ceb.title: Ecumenical Councils and the Pope
ceb.question: Do ecumenical councils have authority over the Pope, or does the Pope override the councils?
ceb.answer: An ecumenical council and the Pope are not rival authorities but form one teaching body: a council is only ecumenical, that is, universally binding, when it acts in union with and is confirmed by the Successor of Peter, the head of the college of bishops. The bishops of the whole world are the successors of the Apostles and, together with the Pope as their head, exercise supreme authority, exactly as the Apostles gathered with Peter at the Council of Jerusalem, where Peter spoke decisively and the assembly wrote, 'It is the decision of the holy Spirit and of us' (Acts 15:28). The Pope cannot be simply overruled by the bishops apart from him, for the college has no authority without its head, just as the body has none without Peter. Neither does the Pope govern in isolation from the bishops; ordinarily he teaches with and through them. This is why the doctrine of conciliarism, that a council stands above the Pope, was rejected. The Church's authority is always Peter-with-the-bishops, never one against the other.

en.answer_full:
> "Peter has spoken through Leo." — Acclamation of the bishops at the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD)

The question of whether councils outrank popes or popes outrank councils frames a false competition. Catholic teaching holds that the Pope and the college of bishops together constitute the supreme authority of the Church — two expressions of one governing subject, never two rival powers. Understanding this requires both careful historical analysis of the conciliarist crisis and precise theological definition of what **episcopal collegiality** means.

---

## The Historical Question: Constance and Basel

### The Crisis of the Great Schism

The Council of Constance (1414–1418) met during the **Great Western Schism**, when three men simultaneously claimed to be the legitimate pope. No unambiguous pope could confirm the council's opening sessions, yet the Church desperately needed a council to restore unity. The decree *Haec Sancta* (1415) asserted that the council held authority "immediately from Christ" and that even the pope was bound to obey it in matters of faith, unity, and reform.

The crucial question is whether *Haec Sancta* represents a permanent dogmatic definition of conciliarism or an emergency instrument for resolving a unique constitutional crisis. Catholic theologians and the subsequent Magisterium have consistently held the latter position for three reasons. First, the decree was promulgated before the council's legitimacy was formally confirmed by a recognized pope. Second, it was never given universal papal ratification as a standing principle of governance. Third, it was immediately followed by the election of Pope Martin V, who deliberately avoided any explicit endorsement of conciliarist theory. The Council of Florence (1439) later defined papal primacy in terms incompatible with strict conciliarism, and the Council of Basel's radical conciliarist wing was condemned as schismatic.

---

## The Biblical Foundation: Acts 15 and the Jerusalem Council

### The Pattern of Collegial Governance

Acts 15 provides the clearest New Testament model of how supreme authority operates in the Church. A serious doctrinal dispute — whether Gentile converts must observe the Mosaic Law — was resolved not by Peter alone, not by the community alone, but by the **apostolic college gathered with Peter**. Peter spoke first and decisively: "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7). James then synthesized and applied the decision. The entire assembly issued the binding decree: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).

The pattern is hierarchical and collegial simultaneously. Peter's testimony is authoritative and settles the doctrinal question. James's summary is accepted. The decree issues from the whole college. This is not a council overriding Peter; it is the apostolic college operating in unity with its head. This is precisely what Vatican II means by **episcopal collegiality**.

### John 21 and Matthew 18

John 21:15–17 commissions Peter as universal shepherd, confirming his primacy over the whole flock. Matthew 18:18 gives the power to bind and loose to all the apostles — the same power given to Peter alone in Matthew 16:19. The two passages do not contradict each other; they show that Peter holds the keys in a way that is unique (as head and focal point of unity) while all the apostles share in collegial governing authority (as members of the college). The college never acts validly *against* its head.

---

## Theological Distinctions

### Collegiality versus Conciliarism

**Episcopal collegiality** is the Catholic doctrine that the college of bishops, in union with the pope as its head, possesses full and supreme authority over the universal Church (*Lumen Gentium* 22). This authority is exercised in two modes: in a solemn way through an ecumenical council, and in an ordinary and universal way through the dispersed teaching of the bishops in communion with Rome.

**Conciliarism** is the heterodox position that the council possesses supreme authority *independently of or over* the pope — that the bishops assembled can validly define doctrine or exercise governing authority without or against the pope's consent. This position was rejected at the Council of Florence (1439), explicitly condemned in the context of Gallicanism and Febronianism, and definitively ruled out by *Pastor Aeternus* at Vatican I (1870).

### The Pope's Authority Relative to Councils

The First Vatican Council defined that the pope's jurisdictional primacy is "truly episcopal, and immediate" and extends to "each and every church and each and every pastor and faithful member." This means the pope's authority does not derive from a council and does not require conciliar ratification. He may act on his own authority in matters of faith and governance.

At the same time, *Pastor Aeternus* was careful not to claim that popes are above councils in the sense of being exempt from doctrinal continuity. A pope cannot define doctrine that contradicts a previously defined council — not because the council overrides him, but because no pope has authority to contradict the deposit of faith, which an ecumenical council authoritatively expresses.

---

## Patristic Testimony

### Leo the Great (c. AD 449–461)

Pope Leo demonstrates the interplay of papal and conciliar authority most clearly at Chalcedon. His *Tome to Flavian* was the theological foundation of the council's definition against Monophysitism. When the bishops heard it read aloud, they acclaimed:

> "This is the faith of the Fathers, this is the faith of the Apostles. So we all believe, thus the orthodox believe. Anathema to him who does not thus believe. Peter has spoken thus through Leo." — Acclamation at Chalcedon (451 AD)

The council did not override Leo; it recognized him as the voice of Peter. Leo later ratified the council's christological definition. The synergy is complete.

### Cyprian of Carthage (c. AD 251)

Cyprian articulates the principle of episcopal unity with its center:

> "The episcopate is one, each part of which is held by each one for the whole. The Church also is one, which is spread abroad far and wide into a multitude by an increase of fruitfulness. As there are many rays of the sun, but one light… so the Church, shone over with the light of the Lord, sheds forth her rays over the whole world, yet it is one light which is everywhere diffused." — *On the Unity of the Church*, 5

For Cyprian, unity of the episcopate requires a center, and that center is the Chair of Peter.

### Innocent I (c. AD 417)

When the African bishops settled the Pelagian controversy at their councils, they referred the matter to Rome for final confirmation. Innocent I's reply makes the primatial claim explicit:

> "In seeking the things of God… you have referred to our judgment, knowing what is due to the Apostolic See, since all we who are set in this place desire to follow the Apostle [Peter] from whom the very episcopate and whole authority of this name has emerged." — *Epistula* 29

---

## Conciliar and Magisterial Definition

The First Vatican Council (*Pastor Aeternus*, 1870) defined:

> "We teach and define… that the Roman Pontiff has supreme and complete power of jurisdiction over the universal Church, not merely in matters pertaining to faith and morals, but also in matters pertaining to the discipline and government of the Church dispersed throughout the whole world."

The Second Vatican Council (*Lumen Gentium* 22, 1964) defined:

> "The order of bishops, which succeeds to the college of apostles and gives this apostolic body continued existence, is also the subject of supreme and full power over the universal Church, provided we understand this body together with its head the Roman Pontiff and never without this head."

| Reference | Teaching |
|---|---|
| CCC 880 | The college of bishops exercises supreme authority in union with the Pope |
| CCC 882 | The Pope has full, supreme, and immediate authority over the whole Church |
| CCC 883 | The college of bishops has no authority without union with the Roman Pontiff |
| CCC 884 | The college exercises power solemnly in an ecumenical council |
| CCC 885 | Bishops govern particular churches as vicars of Christ |

---

## Common Objections

**"The Council of Constance defined that councils are above popes — this is binding Catholic teaching."** The Magisterium has consistently taught that *Haec Sancta* was an emergency measure for a unique crisis, not a universal dogmatic definition. It was never given full papal ratification as a standing principle, and subsequent councils (Florence, Vatican I) definitively rejected conciliarism as a standing ecclesiological theory.

**"If the pope can define doctrine alone, what is the point of councils?"** Councils serve irreplaceable functions: they allow the full episcopal college to deliberate together, they express the faith of the universal Church in a manner of maximum authority, they provide for reception and application of doctrine across the whole Church, and they demonstrate the collegial unity of the episcopate. Papal definitions are rare; councils are the ordinary collegial exercise of supreme authority.

**"The early Church was governed by councils, not popes — the papacy is a medieval invention."** The early Church held councils and referred their results to Rome for confirmation. Nicaea (325) was confirmed by Sylvester I; Chalcedon's definition was authenticated by Leo's Tome. The pattern is not councils alone but pope-and-council from the beginning.

---

## Conclusion

The Catholic teaching is neither that councils supersede popes nor that popes can ignore councils. Pope and council together are two expressions of the single supreme authority Christ gave his Church. The historical experiments with conciliarism arose in crisis and were ultimately rejected; the defined teaching, affirmed at Florence, Vatican I, and Vatican II, holds that the bishop of Rome and the college of bishops in communion with him constitute the indivisible governing subject of the universal Church.
